Do not pair ragg with showtext-only fonts. dev: "ragg_png" --- ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: # From Perfect Mirror to Average Mirror In the idealized world the matrix \( M \) satisfied \( M = M^\top \) exactly. In the real world edges are added and removed, directions flip, measurements are noisy. The instantaneous adjacency matrix is almost never symmetric. Yet if we look at a long-run average — the density of visits, the time-averaged connection strength, the histogram of a chaotic orbit — a clear mirror symmetry can reappear. That is **symmetry on average**. This is the idea from a classic paper *Symmetric Chaos*, by Frame and Golubitsky: {{< pdf https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/golubitsky.4/reprintweb-0.5/output/papers/symmetric_chaos.pdf >}} ## Noisy adjacency that still averages to a mirror ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # ideal mirror ideal <- matrix(0, 6, 6) ideal[1, 2] <- ideal[2, 1] <- 1 ideal[2, 3] <- ideal[3, 2] <- 1 ideal[3, 4] <- ideal[4, 3] <- 1 ideal[4, 5] <- ideal[5, 4] <- 1 ideal[5, 6] <- ideal[6, 5] <- 1 ideal[6, 1] <- ideal[1, 6] <- 1 # many noisy realizations n_real <- 200 avg <- matrix(0, 6, 6) for (k in 1:n_real) { noise <- matrix(rbinom(36, 1, 0.08), 6, 6) noisy <- pmax(0, pmin(1, ideal + noise - matrix(rbinom(36, 1, 0.08), 6, 6))) avg <- avg + noisy } avg <- avg / n_real par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) image(t(ideal[6:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = c("white", "steelblue"), main = "Ideal mirror" ) image(t(noisy[6:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = c("white", "firebrick"), main = "One noisy snapshot" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `noisy[6:1, ]`: ! incorrect number of dimensions ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} image(t(avg[6:1, ]), axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(20, "Blues"), main = "Average over 200 snapshots" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Instantaneous noisy matrix versus its long-run average](03-symmetry-on-average_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: ## Field and Golubitsky’s Design Method Field and Golubitsky generate symmetric images by iterating a map that is *equivariant* under a chosen symmetry group (usually a cyclic or dihedral group of order \( m \)). The basic family of maps (in the complex plane) takes the form \[ z \mapsto \bigl(\lambda + \alpha |z|^2 + \beta \operatorname{Re}(z^m) + i\omega\bigr) z + \gamma \overline{z}^{m-1}. \] - The polynomial is constructed so that it *commutes* with rotation by \( 2\pi/m \) (and, when \( \omega = 0 \), with reflections). That is the mathematical embodiment of the symmetry: if \( z \) is on the attractor then so is every rotated (and reflected) copy. - Iteration of the map is chaotic for many parameter values: a single trajectory wanders aperiodically and never settles into a periodic orbit that itself possesses the symmetry. - The *density* of a long trajectory (how often the orbit visits each pixel) nevertheless inherits the full symmetry of the map. Colouring by visit count therefore produces a picture whose symmetry is visible only “on average.” This is precisely the passage from an idealized mirror constraint to symmetry-on-average in the presence of chaotic “noise.” ### Emperor’s Cloak (pentagonal, \( m = 5 \)) A classic example uses the reduced form in which \( \alpha = -\lambda \) (the complex logistic map plus a symmetry-breaking term): \[ z \mapsto (\lambda - \lambda |z|^2) z + \gamma \overline{z}^{4}. \] ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(grid) # --- Parameters: Emperor's Cloak --------------------------------------- n <- 5 lambda <- -1.806 alpha <- 1.806 beta <- 0 omega <- 0 gamma <- 1 cloak_step <- function(z) { (lambda + alpha * (Re(z)^2 + Im(z)^2) + beta * Re(z^n) + 1i * omega) * z + gamma * Conj(z)^(n - 1) } # --- Many orbits in parallel ------------------------------------------- set.seed(1) n_orbits <- 20000 z <- complex( real = rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1), imaginary = rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1) ) for (i in 1:500) z <- cloak_step(z) # burn-in # --- Pass 1: bounds ----------------------------------------------------- L <- 0 zz <- z for (i in 1:300) { zz <- cloak_step(zz) L <- max(L, abs(Re(zz)), abs(Im(zz))) } L <- L * 1.05 # --- Pass 2: 2D histogram ---------------------------------------------- N <- 800 counts <- numeric(N * N) for (i in 1:1000) { z <- cloak_step(z) ix <- floor((Re(z) + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L iy <- floor((Im(z) + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L ok <- is.finite(ix) & is.finite(iy) & ix >= 1L & ix <= N & iy >= 1L & iy <= N counts <- counts + tabulate((iy[ok] - 1L) * N + ix[ok], nbins = N * N) } # --- Density -> colour -------------------------------------------------- d <- log1p(counts) / log1p(quantile(counts[counts > 0], 0.999)) d <- pmin(d, 1) stops <- c(0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.72, 1) pal <- col2rgb(c("black", "#FFE9FF", "yellow", "red", "#00D600", "white")) ch <- lapply(1:3, function(k) approx(stops, pal[k, ], xout = d)$y) cols <- rgb(ch[[1]], ch[[2]], ch[[3]], maxColorValue = 255) img <- t(matrix(cols, N, N))[N:1, ] # rows = y (top first), cols = x # --- Draw on the active device (Quarto captures this) ------------------ grid.newpage() grid.raster(img, interpolate = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The Emperor's Cloak symmetric icon (Field & Golubitsky).](03-symmetry-on-average_files/figure-html/fig-emperors-cloak-1.png){#fig-emperors-cloak fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(symengine) library(ggplot2) # --- Parameters: Emperor's Cloak --------------------------------------- n <- 5 lambda <- -1.806 alpha <- 1.806 beta <- 0 omega <- 0 gamma <- 1 # --- Symbolic map, using real/imaginary pairs -------------------------- x <- S("x") y <- S("y") cmul <- function(a, b) { list( re = a$re * b$re - a$im * b$im, im = a$re * b$im + a$im * b$re ) } cpow <- function(a, k) { r <- list(re = S("1"), im = S("0")) for (i in seq_len(k)) r <- cmul(r, a) r } zn <- cpow(list(re = x, im = y), n) # z^n zc1 <- cpow(list(re = x, im = -y), n - 1) # conj(z)^(n-1) p <- lambda + alpha * (x^2 + y^2) + beta * zn$re fx <- expand(p * x - omega * y + gamma * zc1$re) fy <- expand(p * y + omega * x + gamma * zc1$im) fx ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Add) -1.806*x + 1.806*x*y^2.0 - 6.0*x^2*y^2 + 1.0*x^4 + 1.806*x^3.0 + 1.0*y^4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} fy # inspect the expanded polynomials (optional) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Add) -1.806*y + 4.0*x*y^3 - 4.0*x^3*y + 1.806*x^2.0*y + 1.806*y^3.0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # --- Turn the symbolic polynomials into plain R functions --------------- to_r_fun <- function(expr) { e <- parse(text = as.character(expr))[[1]] # "**" parses as "^" in R function(x, y) eval(e, list(x = x, y = y)) } f_x <- to_r_fun(fx) f_y <- to_r_fun(fy) # Quick check against a direct complex-number calculation (optional) z0 <- complex(real = 0.3, imaginary = -0.2) z1 <- (lambda + alpha * Mod(z0)^2 + beta * Re(z0^n) + 1i * omega) * z0 + gamma * Conj(z0)^(n - 1) all.equal(c(f_x(0.3, -0.2), f_y(0.3, -0.2)), c(Re(z1), Im(z1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # --- Many orbits in parallel ------------------------------------------- set.seed(1) n_orbits <- 20000 px <- rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1) py <- rnorm(n_orbits, sd = 0.1) iterate <- function() { nx <- f_x(x = px, y = py) ny <- f_y(x = px, y = py) px <<- nx py <<- ny } for (i in 1:500) iterate() # burn-in # Pass 1: bounds L <- 0 sx <- px sy <- py for (i in 1:300) { nx <- f_x(x = sx, y = sy) ny <- f_y(x = sx, y = sy) sx <- nx sy <- ny L <- max(L, abs(sx), abs(sy)) } L <- L * 1.05 # Pass 2: 2D histogram N <- 800 counts <- numeric(N * N) for (i in 1:1000) { iterate() ix <- floor((px + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L iy <- floor((py + L) / (2 * L) * N) + 1L ok <- is.finite(ix) & is.finite(iy) & ix >= 1L & ix <= N & iy >= 1L & iy <= N counts <- counts + tabulate((iy[ok] - 1L) * N + ix[ok], nbins = N * N) } # --- ggplot2 ------------------------------------------------------------- centres <- seq(-L, L, length.out = N + 1)[-1] - L / N cloak <- data.frame( x = rep(centres, times = N), # ix varies fastest, matching the count index y = rep(centres, each = N), d = pmin(1, log1p(counts) / log1p(quantile(counts[counts > 0], 0.999))) ) ggplot(cloak, aes(x, y, fill = d)) + geom_raster() + scale_fill_gradientn( colours = c("black", "#FFE9FF", "yellow", "red", "#00D600", "white"), values = c(0, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.72, 1), limits = c(0, 1), guide = "none" ) + coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) + theme_void() + theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", colour = NA)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The Emperor's Cloak, built with symengine and drawn with ggplot2.](03-symmetry-on-average_files/figure-html/fig-emperors-cloak-symengine-1.png){#fig-emperors-cloak-symengine fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: ### p5.js: live Emperor’s Cloak ```{=html}

Emperor’s Cloak accumulating in real time. The five-fold symmetry appears only in the density.

``` ### A second design (triangular symmetry) The same construction with \( m = 3 \) and different coefficients yields a triangular icon. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} icon3 <- function(z, lambda = 1.5, alpha = -1.0, gamma = -0.8) { r2 <- Mod(z)^2 (lambda + alpha * r2) * z + gamma * Conj(z)^2 } n <- 100000 z <- 0.2 + 0.1i pts <- complex(n) for (i in 1:n) { z <- icon3(z) pts[i] <- z } pts <- pts[-(1:1000)] pts <- pts[abs(pts) < 1.6] df <- data.frame(x = Re(pts), y = Im(pts)) ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + stat_bin2d(bins = 70) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "log10", na.value = "black") + coord_fixed() + theme_void() + theme( legend.position = "none", plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Triangular symmetric icon (m = 3)](03-symmetry-on-average_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: The choice of the equivariant polynomial fixes the mathematical symmetry; the chaotic iteration supplies the randomness; the coloured density reveals the symmetry on average. That is the entire Field–Golubitsky design pipeline. # The Three-World Summary | World | Matrix relation | Visual character | |--------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------| | Graphs & adjacency | \( A \) arbitrary | Directed, possibly one-way | | Idealized mirror | \( M = M^\top \) exactly | Perfect bilateral / dihedral | | Real world | \( \mathbb{E}[A] \approx M \) | Symmetry visible only on average | The artistic and design lesson is unchanged from the Field–Golubitsky pictures: you may design with an equivariant rule (a “mirror” constraint) even when the underlying process is noisy or chaotic. The long-term image, the density, the average, will still carry the symmetry you imposed. That is the practical bridge between the clean adjacency algebra and the hurly-burly of generative art.
